questions.question: Where must the 'package' declaration be positioned in a Kotlin file?
options: At the very bottom of the file
As the very first non-comment statement at the top of the file
Inside the fun main() block
It can be placed anywhere randomly in the file
questions.hint: Think about where the postal address is placed on a letter.
questions.explanation: In Kotlin, if a package header is present, it must be the very first non-comment declaration at the top of the file.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using packages in a large Kotlin application?
options: To speed up internet download rates
To group related files together and prevent name collisions
To make functions private to the entire world
To compress files on disk
questions.hint: Consider having two classes with the same name.
questions.explanation: Packages organize code into logical namespaces and prevent naming conflicts when two files define elements with identical names.

questions.question: Which of the following packages is imported automatically by the Kotlin compiler into every file?
options: kotlin.*
java.sql.*
androidx.compose.*
org.apache.commons.*
questions.explanation: The Kotlin compiler automatically imports default packages like kotlin.*, kotlin.collections.*, and java.lang.* into every source file.

questions.question: What distinguishes an expression from a statement in Kotlin?
options: A statement produces a value, while an expression never does
An expression evaluates to a value that can be assigned or passed, while a statement simply performs an action
Statements can only be written in uppercase
Expressions are only used in database queries
questions.hint: Think about whether a result is returned.
questions.explanation: An expression evaluates to a result value (e.g., '10 + 20' or 'if (a > b) a else b'), whereas a statement performs an action without returning an assignable value.

questions.question: How does Kotlin handle 'if-else' compared to traditional Java or C?
options: Kotlin does not support if-else at all
In Kotlin, 'if' is an expression that returns a value, replacing the ternary operator
Kotlin requires if statements to be terminated with three semicolons
In Kotlin, 'if' can only check boolean numbers
questions.hint: In Kotlin, 'val x = if (...) a else b' is standard syntax.
questions.explanation: In Kotlin, 'if' is an expression that yields a value, which makes traditional ternary operators ('? :') unnecessary.

questions.question: When using 'if' as an expression (e.g., assigning it to a variable), what rule is mandatory?
options: The 'else' branch is strictly required
Parentheses around conditions are forbidden
The condition must be an integer
It must be wrapped in a while loop
questions.hint: The variable must always receive a valid value in all scenarios.
questions.explanation: When 'if' is used as an expression, having an 'else' branch is mandatory so that the variable is guaranteed to be assigned a value in every possible case.

questions.question: Which comment style in Kotlin allows nesting multiple comments inside each other?
options: Single-line comments (//)
Multi-line block comments (/* ... */)
Hash comments (#)
HTML comments (<!-- -->)
questions.explanation: Kotlin supports nested block comments (/* ... /* ... */ ... */), allowing developers to comment out large blocks containing existing comments without compilation errors.

questions.question: What is the recommended naming convention for Kotlin variables and functions?
options: SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE
kebab-case
camelCase
PascalCase
questions.hint: Starts lowercase and capitalizes each subsequent word.
questions.explanation: Kotlin coding conventions recommend 'camelCase' for variable and function identifiers (e.g., calculateTotal, studentAge).

questions.question: Are semicolons mandatory at the end of each line of code in Kotlin?
options: Yes, every single statement must end with a semicolon
No, semicolons are optional and omitted by standard convention
Only when writing functions
Only when writing string variables
questions.explanation: In Kotlin, semicolons are optional and generally omitted unless multiple statements are written on the same physical line.

questions.question: What is a 'top-level declaration' in Kotlin?
options: Code that can only be executed by the operating system kernel
A function, property, or class declared directly inside a file outside of any wrapping class
A comment written on line 1
A variable that cannot be read
questions.hint: In Kotlin, you do not need a dummy class wrapper just to hold a function or constant.
questions.explanation: Top-level declarations are functions, properties, or classes written directly in a source file without needing an enclosing class.
